extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, diplomats, international law and security researchers, and civil-society actors interested in lethal autonomous weapons and multilateral regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical summary of India's policy and normative positions on lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS) at multilateral forums, especially within the CCW/GGE context. Useful for understanding India's preferences on forum, definitions, legal approach, and preferred regulatory instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of International Humanitarian Law (IHL) to LAWS
rubrics_metrics.description: IHL’s rules and principles take a technology-neutral approach and fully apply to LAWS; weapons should be regulated based on the effects of their use rather than the underlying technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues IHL offers a sufficient framework for regulating LAWS, citing the CCW’s five protocols (e.g., Protocol IV prohibiting blinding laser weapons) as examples of effects-based regulation. It notes state parties have affirmed that responsibility and accountability for using LAWS lie with human operators, reinforcing reliance on existing IHL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-tier approach toward LAWS
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between systems that are not compliant with IHL (to be prohibited) and systems that could potentially be made compliant (to be regulated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The GGE is working on this two-tier approach; India references it as a guiding framework. The approach implies prohibiting clearly non-compliant systems while regulating or permitting systems that can meet IHL requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a common definition/characterization before pursuing a binding instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: Calls for a legally binding instrument are premature until states agree on a common definition and characterization of LAWS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: India emphasizes arriving at a definition first, citing the long-unadopted 1996 draft Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism as an example where lack of definition stalled adoption. The GGE compiled a non-exhaustive list of state-submitted definitions and is working toward common elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for a political declaration as a pragmatic first step
rubrics_metrics.description: A high-level political declaration can spur national policies and regulatory frameworks and serve as an interim or complementary measure to a treaty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on the 2019 guiding principles, India has supported a political declaration; the United States’ 2023 voluntary political declaration on responsible use of AI and autonomy in the military is cited as an example of this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human responsibility and accountability principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsibility and accountability for the use of LAWS should remain with human operators and decision-makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State parties to the CCW have affirmed this principle, which India cites to argue against alternative regulatory frameworks that might diffuse or remove human accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects- or end-use-focused regulation (not technology bans)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation should concentrate on specific end uses or weapon effects (e.g., systems causing superfluous injury or indiscriminate harm) rather than banning the enabling technologies themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay notes that AI-enabled autonomy can be a function rather than a weapon; thus, rules should target problematic end uses. It references the UNIDIR observation that military AI use cases extend beyond weapons to logistics and data processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build upon existing CCW framework and protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the CCW and its mechanisms (including Article 8, which enables adoption of new protocols) as the basis for any new regulatory instrument on LAWS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With 127 state parties, the CCW is presented as the appropriate instrument; the GGE’s eleven guiding principles and prior CCW work should be the foundation for future elements or protocols regulating LAWS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating parallel forums; prioritize the GGE/consensus process
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent duplication of effort and fragmentation by keeping discussions within the GGE under the CCW rather than opening parallel processes (e.g., at the UNGA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: India voted against the December 2023 UNGA resolution, arguing it would duplicate resources; it believes the GGE has succeeded in bringing stakeholders together and has produced a substantive body of work to build upon. The essay also notes criticisms that consensus rules can be used by some states to stall binding regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of legal, military, and technical expertise in drafting instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Any formulation of elements for an instrument should account for legal, military, and technical expertise to ensure practicality and compliance with IHL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The GGE plans to work toward formulating 'a set of elements of an instrument' based on existing CCW protocols and informed by multidisciplinary expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid blanket condemnation; weigh potential benefits of autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Blanket condemnation of autonomous technologies is counterproductive and may stigmatize beneficial military applications (e.g., increased precision, efficiency, reduced human error).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay urges recognition of positive effects and cautions against stigmatizing technology that can be used beneficially in logistics, data processing, or precision targeting; regulation should be nuanced and targeted to harmful end uses.
